synopsis: Ramen before class, and the shop's hand-brushed wall menu has no pictures. Shin reads it like a picture book, cracking each character into a memory image and saying plainly which parts he is only guessing at. The catch lands warm: he can decode what a dish is, but not what a person wants, so the reading only works once it meets someone's likes and a no-meat request. The learner uses his component route to order for themselves.

forbiddenClaims: surname, guessed kana name, nationality, or private history
heritage reduced to a stereotype or a punchline
asserted kanji etymology stated as fact
surname, guessed kana name, nationality, job, or private history

scenes.goal: Decode a pictureless hand-brushed ramen menu by kanji components, and reach the point where knowing what a dish is does not tell you what a person wants.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When the expert can read every character, is that enough to order for someone else?
scenes.learnerNeed: A kanji-decoding and preference-ordering task where reading the menu only becomes useful once it meets someone's likes and a dietary limit.

nodes.description: A cramped ramen counter before class. The whole wall is a hand-brushed menu: black characters on cream paper, no photos, no prices in numerals anyone can find fast. Steam curls up past the last empty stools.

nodes.attentionTarget: the whole hand-brushed wall of characters

nodes.intent: Crack one scary character into a memory image aloud, flag openly that it may be nonsense rather than the real origin, and land that it is now unforgettable.
nodes.attentionTarget: the single character 肉 at the top of the menu

It might be complete nonsense. But once you've pictured it that way, you'll never forget it again, will you?

nodes.intent: Read the easy shape-and-meaning characters with certainty, then openly hedge on a reading he is only half-sure of, keeping the meaning and the reading honestly separate.
nodes.attentionTarget: the size characters 大 and 小 and the compound 半熟

nodes.attentionTarget: the row of dish names he cannot yet sort

nodes.resume: Shin has decoded what each dish is and handed the preference choice back. The learner steps in to read the meat-free line with his component route, say what they like, and order aloud with a counter — including a no-meat bowl for Robert.

nodes.resumeContext: The wall menu has 肉 dishes on one side and 魚 and 野菜 dishes on the other. The learner uses Shin's shape-first component route to read a dish name, states a preference with 〜が好き, orders their own bowl with a counter (ラーメン一杯 / ひとつ), and asks 「肉が入っていないもの、ありますか」 so Robert gets a meat-free bowl — pairing the decoding with an actual want rather than choosing one dish as universally best.

nodes.description: One dish name lifts off the wall and splits into its left and right parts, side by side. Only the piece that went unread returns for another try; the parts already decoded stay in place, and the counter phrase waits underneath.

nodes.resume: The learner has read a dish, said what they like, and ordered — one meat-free bowl for Robert included. Shin looks pleased that the reading only did its job once it met a preference.

nodes.description: The wall menu no longer reads as a solid block. The 肉 dishes sit in one column, the 魚 and 野菜 dishes in another, and the meat-free bowl the learner picked out is circled in chalk. The steam behind the counter thickens as an order is called back.

scenes.goal: Let Shin hand over the method rather than the answer, so his decoding becomes a shared tool and each person's likes decide their own bowl.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can an expert's skill be more useful handed over than performed?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how to use Shin's decoding method — take the answer, or take the route.

nodes.description: Everyone has claimed a stool along the counter. One dish name near the bottom of the wall is still unread, and Shin taps it with the end of his pencil instead of saying it.

nodes.intent: Deliberately withhold the answer and offer the route instead — left half, right half — inviting the learner to decode the last character themselves.
nodes.attentionTarget: the last unread dish name and its two halves

nodes.question: How do you use Shin's method for the last character?

options.action: Ask Shin to just read it out so you can order faster.

japaneseByBand.n1: Shinさん、そこはもう先に読んじゃってもらえます?早いとこ頼みたいんで。

nodes.resume: The learner has chosen whether to take Shin's answer or his route. Either way the last dish gets read and the orders go in, Robert's meat-free bowl among them.

nodes.intent: Place his own order for the meat-free bowl with a counter, warm and relieved to be able to ask for it plainly.
nodes.attentionTarget: the fish bowl the learner circled for him

nodes.intent: Close on his own theme: the character is the easy part, even a made-up memory sticks, but what a person likes is the one thing only they can decide — and that is the hard part.
nodes.attentionTarget: the circled meat-free bowl and the now-readable wall

n1.japanese: ほら、もう忘れないって。——字なんてね、正直いつだって簡単なんだよ。でたらめな覚え方でも、一回はまれば忘れない。ただ、何が好きかだけは、どうやったって自分で決めるしかなくてね。結局そこが、一番むずかしい。
n1.reading: ほら、もうわすれないって。——じなんてね、しょうじきいつだってかんたんなんだよ。でたらめなおぼえかたでも、いっかいはまればわすれない。ただ、なにがすきかだけは、どうやったってじぶんできめるしかなくてね。けっきょくそこが、いちばんむずかしい。
n1.english: See, you won't forget it. — Characters, honestly, are always easy. Even a nonsense way of remembering, once it sticks, it stays. It's just that what you like is the one thing you've simply got to decide for yourself, however you go about it. In the end, that's the hardest part.

nodes.description: Bowls land along the counter, one to each stool. Robert's meat-free bowl sits among them, no different to look at. Behind the diners the wall menu stays legible now — two columns, one circled line — the way Shin left it.

outcomes.description: The class orders from a pictureless hand-brushed menu by decoding kanji as memory images; the reading only becomes useful once it is paired with each diner's likes and a no-meat request, and Shin hands over the route rather than the answer.

Shin is introduced as the class's kanji reader through his running joke that every character is easy; the chapter establishes that his expertise carries visible uncertainty — he decodes what a dish is and openly hedges a reading, but cannot decode what a person wants, so his skill only works once it meets a preference.
Express-likes-and-order-from-a-pictureless-menu-by-decoding-kanji evidence returns through the registered transfer activity; the story emits no lesson-completion command.

replay.withdrawnContentFallback: Use the same kanji-decode and preference-ordering beats with neutral nameplates and a generic reader who decodes a pictureless menu as memory images, hedges one reading openly, and hands the preference and no-meat choice back to each diner.
